title: Psalm 134:1–3
context: A Song of Ascents and the last of the pilgrim songs: servants of the LORD who stand by night in the house of the LORD are called to bless Him, lifting hands to the holy place. The answering benediction asks the LORD—Maker of heaven and earth—to bless from Zion.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on night ministry in the LORD’s house, lifted hands in blessing, and the Creator’s benediction from Zion—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Psalm 134:1–3.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD. Servant—peculiarly so called, priests and Levites. Night—not only by day, but also by night, when their watch was more necessary. Stand—serve or minister. Lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD. The LORD that made heaven and earth bless thee out of Zion. Thee—thee whosoever thou art who dost faithfully perform the duty here commanded.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Psalm 134)

reformed.quote: Behold! bless ye Jehovah. The Levites are addressed as servants of God from the functions they discharged, appointed by turns to watch by night in the Temple. Many, through abuse of ceremonies, thought nothing more necessary than standing idly in the Temple, and overlooked the principal part of their duty. Merely to keep nightly watch, kindle lamps, and superintend sacrifices was of no importance unless they served God spiritually and referred all outward ceremonies to the main sacrifice—the celebration of God’s praises. Lift up your hands: why do men lift hands when they pray, if not that hearts may be raised at the same time to God? Jehovah bless thee out of Zion! Priests were to bless the people in His name, leading the way in divine service as representing Christ’s person. The God who blesses out of Zion is also Creator of heaven and earth—His title as Creator sets forth power so that nothing may not be hoped from Him; Zion’s nearness invites approach with the confidence of those welcomed to a Father’s bosom.
reformed.source: Commentary on the Book of Psalms (on Psalm 134)

verses.text: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!
verses.arminianNotes:
Come, bless the LORD—all servants who stand by night in His house. Priests and Levites are peculiarly named; night watch makes the call more urgent.

Classical Arminians hear a real summons to praise. Serving is more than occupying the courts; bless Him while you stand, day or night.
verses.reformedNotes:
Behold, bless Jehovah—night watchers in the Temple urged beyond idle ceremony to spiritual praise as the main sacrifice.

Reformed accent: outward standing without heart-praise abuses holy place. God requires the celebration of His name from those He stationed at night.
verses.keyContrast: Both call night servants in the LORD’s house to bless Him. Arminians typically stress faithful ministry that actually praises while it watches; Reformed readers typically stress spiritual service over idle ceremony, with praise as the chief sacrifice of the night watch.

verses.text: Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!
verses.arminianNotes:
Lift hands to the holy place and bless the LORD. Gesture and voice join in sanctuary praise.

Arminian pastoral: raise hands and heart together. Blessing God in the holy place is the duty night servants must not neglect for empty conversation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Lift up your hands—and with them the heart—to God, and bless Him. The form of calling on the Name rebukes careless standing or vain talk in the Temple.

Reformed note: bodily lifting without raised affection is hollow. Proper worship joins posture and spirit before the Holy One.

verses.text: May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!
verses.arminianNotes:
May the LORD bless you from Zion—He who made heaven and earth. Blessing returns to whoever faithfully does the duty commanded.

Classical Arminians welcome the exchange: servants bless the LORD; He blesses the faithful from Zion. The Creator’s scope matches the nearness of His house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jehovah bless thee out of Zion—Creator of heaven and earth. Priests bless the people in His name as representing Christ; Creator power invites large hope, Zion nearness invites Fatherly access.

Reformed comfort: look to the heavens for dominion, to Zion for near love. The benediction is God’s, not a license for the people to sleep while others chant.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear blessing from Zion by the Maker of heaven and earth. Arminians typically stress the reciprocal gift to whoever faithfully performs the commanded duty; Reformed readers typically stress priestly blessing in Christ’s name, joining Creator power with Zion’s fatherly nearness.
